content: The arcuate uterus is a type of uterine anomaly characterized by a concave contour of the uterine fundus that extends toward the uterine cavity. Normally, the uterine fundus appears straight or convex on anterior-posterior imaging. However, in the case of an arcuate uterus, the fundus dips into the cavity and may form a small septation. The distinction between an arcuate uterus and a septate uterus is not standardized. The uterus develops during embryogenesis through the fusion of the two Müllerian ducts. During this process, a resorption phase eliminates the partition between the two ducts, creating a single uterine cavity. This resorption begins caudally and progresses cranially. An arcuate uterus represents an incomplete resorption process during the final stages of this development. Most studies on uterine malformations are based on populations of women who have experienced pregnancy loss, which does not provide an accurate prevalence rate in the general population. A screening study by Woelfer et al. found that approximately 5% of women without a history of reproductive problems had an arcuate uterus. In this study, an arcuate uterus was defined as any fundal protrusion into the cavity with an apical angle greater than 90 degrees. The condition may remain undetected in affected individuals and may not result in any reproductive issues, allowing for normal pregnancies. There is no consensus on the relationship between an arcuate uterus and recurrent pregnancy loss. Some experts consider it a normal anatomical variation, while others view it as a pathological condition. Certain studies suggest that an arcuate uterus may be associated with an increased risk of miscarriage, preterm birth, and fetal malpresentation. For example, Woelfer found that the risk of miscarriage is more pronounced in the second trimester. However, the prevalence of arcuate uterus in the general population is similar to that in women undergoing sterilization and lower than in women with recurrent pregnancy loss. A pelvic examination will not reveal the presence of an arcuate uterus. Investigations are typically initiated due to reproductive problems. Diagnostic techniques include transvaginal ultrasonography, sonohysterography, hysterosalpingography, MRI, and hysteroscopy. Recently, 3D ultrasonography has been advocated as an excellent non-invasive method for delineating the condition. Management of an arcuate uterus often does not require surgical intervention, as many patients do not experience reproductive problems. However, in cases of recurrent pregnancy loss thought to be caused by an arcuate uterus, hysteroscopic resection may be performed. The primary differential diagnosis for an arcuate uterus is a uterine septum. The lack of consensus on how to differentiate these two entities complicates the interpretation of results in the medical literature.
